stimulus.text: The third page of the engrossed Constitution, signed at Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, carries the end of Article II and the start of Article III. It says the person with the most electoral votes shall be President “if such Number be a Majority of the whole Number of Electors appointed,” and that if no person has a majority, “the House of Representatives shall in like Manner chuse the President” from the five highest on the list. Section 2 names the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States” and gives power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties” and to appoint ambassadors and “Judges of the supreme Court.” Article III, Section 1 vests judicial power in “one supreme Court,” and says judges “shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour” and that their pay “shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.”
stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the United States, third page, engrossed by Jacob Shallus, signed September 17, 1787. Public domain.

primary_sources: Constitution of the United States, Article II and Article III (September 17, 1787)

stem: The page says judges “shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour” and that their pay “shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.” What was the purpose of those two rules?

options.text: To let judges serve only while the president approves of their rulings
options.misconception: Life tenure during good behaviour frees judges from the president, not the reverse.

options.text: To protect judges from pressure by the president or Congress
To give judges the power to veto laws passed by Congress
options.misconception: Judges do not veto laws; the veto belongs to the president.

options.text: To require judges to retire at a fixed age
options.misconception: Good behaviour sets no age limit; judges serve as long as they behave well.

rationales.B: Background: a judge who cannot be fired or docked in pay for an unpopular ruling can decide cases on the law alone.
rationales.A: Good behaviour tenure means judges do not serve at the president’s pleasure.
rationales.C: The veto is the president’s check on Congress, not a judicial power.
rationales.D: The page sets no retirement age; it ties tenure to behaviour.
rationales.general:
1. The page gives federal judges tenure during good behaviour, not a fixed term.
2. It also forbids cutting their pay while they serve.
3. A judge who cannot be removed or punished in pay for a ruling is free to rule against the powerful.
4. So both rules shield the judiciary from the other two branches.
Remember: life tenure and protected pay are independence, written as rules.
